name: Victor Wagner

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to employers or AI firms. This is confidential. What is a normal workday like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I teach saxophone two days a week at the music school, play with a hotel group on Sundays and record horn parts for local adverts. I have a music bachelor's and enough years on the instrument to teach beginners, though I'm no star soloist.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What is the household relying on?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Hana works at a grocery shop, and we have two school-age children and a mortgage. My music pay is low, similar jobs nearby are scarce, and we have less than a month's expenses saved.

say: I'd say **live saxophone** still gives hotel guests a reason to listen.
I'd ask for **written dates** before counting another Sunday fee.
think: Our **thin savings** make ordinary cancellations a mortgage problem.
Hana's **grocery wage** covers food but cannot replace my teaching days.
do: Confirm **two school days** and four Sunday hotel dates in writing this week.
Keep **Wednesday and Friday pupils** while the school renews their slots.
Delay the **new mouthpiece** until paid Sundays cover scheduled bills.
feel: I feel **anxious** about the mortgage even when AI barely changes work.
S0.quote: The hotel can cancel a Sunday; our mortgage cannot cancel a Monday.
fieldNote: His **thin reserve** and mortgage make a routine booking loss serious even in Plateau.
He avoids **AI tools** and relies on signed school and hotel dates for the household plan.

steps.text: Confirm two school days and four hotel Sundays in writing
Keep Wednesday and Friday sax pupils
Delay new mouthpiece until paid hotel Sundays cover scheduled bills

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the hotel band that a neat rota is pleasant, but nobody buys a table to watch the rota. I would keep teaching saxophone on Wednesdays and Fridays and playing the Sunday set.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I do not use AI and don't see a need to start for a small office saving. We have less than a month of expenses saved, and Hana's grocery pay covers food but not the mortgage without my lessons.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This week I'll ask the music school to confirm next term's two teaching days and ask the hotel for the next four Sunday dates in writing. If those dates pay, I'll put twenty from each fee into a bills account before ordering a new mouthpiece.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious even with little AI change. One lost teaching day would send us to the mortgage lender before we had time to find another school.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What did the cancelled Sunday mean at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The hotel cancelled a Sunday when its dining room closed for repairs. We delayed the children's sports fees until a recording job paid the next week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How do you talk about uncertain dates with Hana?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell Hana the difference between a booking and a possibility. Our older child hears enough money talk already without us pretending a hotel date is signed. The hotel can cancel a Sunday; our mortgage cannot cancel a Monday.

say: I'd ask for a written **school hours plan** before a new feedback system starts.
I'd tell parents a **person's lesson** still needs a paid teacher.
think: **Arrangements and examples** make a third of my fee and may stop.
Combined **beginner classes** could remove more hours when we have almost no reserve.
do: Get the **spring school plan** and ask two nearby schools about real tutor openings this month.
Apply in the **first shift year** only if paid hours fall, degree qualifies, pickup fits and net pay replaces lost fees.
Seek **hotel setup hours** only if manager confirms paid rate and schedule when no tutor job opens.
feel: I feel **alarmed** because likely arrangement losses could hit the mortgage quickly.
S1.quote: A feedback printout cannot stand beside a child whose saxophone squeals.
fieldNote: He expects **one-third income loss** from high-exposure thinking tasks, so the mood rises despite calm speech.
His **job search** requires actual vacancies, qualifying degree, family pickup and net pay.

steps.text: Get written spring hours; keep current pupils until a real paid offer
Apply first shift-year if hours fall: posted degree-qualifying tutor role, pickup, net-after-travel pay replacing loss
Seek hotel setup shifts only with written paid rate and schedule

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the school that software can write practice sheets, but it must say what happens to paid teaching hours. I would ask parents to pay for a lesson with a person, not just a feedback printout. A feedback printout cannot stand beside a child whose saxophone squeals.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I earn about a third of my fee from basic horn arrangements and recorded examples. Those screen tasks could go quickly, and the school could combine beginner classes; we have no spare month to absorb either change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I'll ask the school director for a written spring hours plan and call two nearby schools about posted sax tutor days. In the first year of the shift, if paid hours fall, I'll apply only where my degree qualifies and net pay after travel and the children's pickup covers the lost hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel alarmed because I expect the small arrangements to stop, and that would cut our pay before a new school hires me. I don't enjoy auditions, but I would go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Are there sax tutor openings right now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: One nearby school advertised a tutor last year, but there is no opening this week. I would keep my current pupils while asking for vacancy notices, not quit for a rumour.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What could you do if no music post opens?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If no music post opens, I would ask the hotel about extra paid setup work. I could carry cases and set stands, but only if the manager puts hours and rate in writing.

I'd keep **human lessons** while families still book them.
think: **AGI in 2028** could remove demo fees before robot players arrive around 2031.
Hana's **grocery wage** cannot carry the mortgage after a major cut to my school hours.
do: Get written **school and hotel dates** and total last year's arrangement fees now.
Review **written full interest** with Hana before accepting mortgage relief if school hours halve in first year after 2028.
Keep **current pupils** until a posted qualifying tutor job offers written replacement net pay after travel with pickup covered.
feel: I feel **alarmed** because a lost school day would outlast our savings.
S2.quote: Less than one month's savings will not carry a long wait for a vacancy.
fieldNote: He separates **2028 desk-fee loss** from robot performance risk around 2031.
His **lender and school** plans both require full costs and a real, qualifying paid opening.

steps.text: Get written school/hotel dates before 2028; keep pupils until written qualifying job offer
Review full written interest with Hana before relief if hours halve after 2028
Apply after 2028: posted degree-qualifying tutor role, pickup, written net-after-travel pay replacing loss

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the hotel band that AGI by 2028 could make every demo I sell, so our paid Sunday dates need to be signed now. I would still teach pupils while families want a real saxophone player beside them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Full AGI in 2028 could arrange, edit and prepare beginner lessons more cheaply than I can. Robots able to play hands-on music arrive around 2031, but the demo and planning fees could end first; Hana's grocery wage will not cover our mortgage alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This week I'll ask the school and hotel for written dates and total last year's arrangement fees. In the first year after 2028, if school hours halve, I'll ask the mortgage lender about a temporary plan and apply for a posted nearby tutor job only if my degree qualifies, pickup works and written net pay after travel replaces the loss.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel alarmed because a halved school schedule would leave us short every month. I can make calls to nearby schools, but none has offered a post. Less than one month's savings will not carry a long wait for a vacancy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you accept any payment relief the lender offers?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the lender for the full interest cost before changing a payment. Hana and I would sign nothing until we understood what the smaller monthly bill adds later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there a nearby tutor job available now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No nearby school has promised me a role. I'd keep the pupils I have and apply only when an advertised day actually opens.

say: I'd ask for a **paid two-term band** with a school room and working instruments.
I'd keep **individual lessons** if eight families do not pay.
think: **AGI in 2031** threatens arrangements before robot players arrive around 2034.
**Simple demo fees** may fade earlier, leaving our mortgage exposed.
do: Seek a **signed two-term fee** and free room next spring, with school-funded instrument repairs.
Run the **band class** only with eight paid families and enough working instruments after school-funded repairs.
Renew the **band** in first year after 2031 only if eight repay and room and fee remain.
feel: I feel **anxious** because demo fees may disappear before the new class proves itself.
S3.quote: A room of unpaid chairs will not make a school band.
fieldNote: His **eight-family threshold** and school-funded repairs keep the class from raiding mortgage cash.
He recognises **early demo loss** even with a five-year warning, so anxious remains warranted.

steps.text: Seek signed school band fee, free room and funded repairs
Run band with repaired working instruments and eight paid families; otherwise refund and keep lessons
Renew school band first year after 2031 if eight repay and room and fee remain

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the hotel group that five years is time to secure a paid room for children to play together. I would ask the music school for a two-term band class rather than another screen exercise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: AGI in 2031 could take arrangement and feedback work, with robots that can play around 2034. I think the simple horn-demo fees will fade before 2031 under ordinary software, so we still have a mortgage problem while planning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Next spring I'll ask the school for a signed two-term beginner band fee and a free classroom. If eight families pay for the first term, I'll run it; in the first year after 2031, I'll renew only if eight families pay again and the school keeps the room and fee.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious because a band class can be tested over five years, but the demos may go sooner. I need actual enrolment before telling Hana we have a replacement wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who pays to repair the instruments?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The school owns enough instruments if it repairs two old saxophones first. I would not pay for repairs from our mortgage account; I'd ask the school to sign for that cost.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if only five families enrol?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If only five families enrol, I'd return their money and keep the individual lessons. A room of unpaid chairs will not make a school band.

I'd keep **signed hotel work** that pays the household bills.
think: At **53**, I need work when AGI arrives in 2036.
**Arrangement fees** may vanish before robot players arrive around 2039.

S4.quote: I cannot save from an unsigned concert.
fieldNote: His **thin reserve** makes even ten years feel short while the mortgage is due monthly.
He will not treat a **budget discussion** as a funded three-term contract.

Keep signed hotel dates while saving toward three months

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the school that a decade is enough time to build children who can play together, if the teacher is paid for the hours. I would still take hotel dates that put real money in the account.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll be 53 when AGI arrives in 2036 and robots may play around 2039. Arrangement fees could dry up years before then, so I need steadier lessons and a small mortgage reserve, not a promise that music will somehow survive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I'll ask the school for a written three-term teaching contract if it can fund one, and I'll keep hotel dates only when a fee is signed. By 2036 I'll aim for three months of expenses saved from those paid hours; in the first year after AGI, I'll keep the class only if school funding renews and enough families still pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious because the next mortgage date doesn't wait for 2036. Ten years is useful for asking for stable hours, but I cannot save from an unsigned concert.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is a three-term contract something the school can promise?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The school board sets the music budget each year. I would ask for its decision before calling a three-term contract secure, and I would not resign from current pupils for a discussion.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if it funds only one term?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the school will not fund three terms, I would take the existing paid term and ask the hotel about confirmed Sundays. I would not borrow for a new instrument to impress either employer.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because demos and paid lesson preparation could vanish before I find another qualifying music post. A signed school schedule, honest lender costs and a real vacancy with pay that covers travel and pickup would help us hold the mortgage.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask how a child hears a wrong note without being ashamed. I can sit beside a child and try the passage again; that is part of what a family pays for.

headlineQuote: I can sit beside a child and try the passage again; that is part of what a family pays for.
portrait: Victor is a **43-year-old** experienced saxophonist with a music bachelor's, school lessons, hotel shows and local recording work.
He never uses **AI tools**, and low pay, few local jobs, two children and thin savings make the mortgage fragile.
He expects **demo and planning** fees to fall before robots reach live playing three years after each AGI date.
He seeks **written school hours** and a paid band class with eight enrolled families, funded instruments and renewed fees.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** worries him most because demo and preparation fees may vanish before another paid post opens.
whatWouldHelp: A **signed school schedule**, clear lender costs and a qualifying vacancy with enough net pay would protect mortgage payments.
